description:
About Me and My Interests: Building MarsWalk Planner for NASA Space Apps 2026! I'm a developer passionate about space tech, mapping real Jezero Crater data into safety-first Martian spacewalk routes.

Why Join Our Team: We foster a collaborative environment focused on space exploration and real-world problem-solving. Join us to turn bold interplanetary survival ideas into reality!
summary: MarsWalk Planner is a safety-first route planner for Mars spacewalks (EVAs), built on real data from Jezero crater. A crew on foot is only as safe as its walk home, so for every point on the map the app computes how many minutes the walk back to the habitat takes. A stop is allowed only if the walk home fits the reserve; other stops are refused, with the reason. USGS HiRISE terrain, a CTX orbital photo, THEMIS thermal inertia, radiation, suit failure and daylight come together in one full-screen map and a helmet HUD view. Every result is also shown as a range, because walking speed in a suit is the least certain number. It runs offline in one HTML file on a laptop, tablet or phone. Built for the challenge "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map".
details:
The problem

A crew on foot on Mars is only as safe as its walk home. If a suit, rover or habitat system fails, the crew has to get back on foot with the oxygen and power they have left. So a route map has to answer not "what is the shortest path?" but "from where can we still get home in time?"

What we built

MarsWalk Planner computes the walking time from every cell of a terrain model back to the habitat (uphill is slower; steep, rough and soft ground is penalised; slope limits depend on the crew mode). A sortie may only visit places inside the walk-back limit; stops outside it are refused, with the reason. The app also shows the cosmic-ray dose along the route, whether shelter can be reached within a solar-storm warning, a suit-failure scenario (two crew sharing one suit's supply walk slower, so the limit shrinks from 120 to 48 minutes), the daylight left before sunset, and a first-person helmet view with a HUD (compass, walk-home time against the limit, EVA time left, dose) for any moment of the mission clock.

Real data

The app opens on a 12 by 12 km window of Jezero crater built from the USGS Mars 2020 HiRISE terrain model (2 m), with the CTX orbital photo, THEMIS thermal inertia and NASA's real Perseverance traverse. Ground roughness is measured at the native 2 m resolution before the map is averaged to 20-40 m cells.

Benefits and intended impact

Before a sortie starts, planners can see where a crew can still get home in time, which stops fail that rule and why, and how much the answer depends on each assumption. That makes the trade-off between reach, reserve and risk visible and easy to discuss. Any other height grid can be loaded (exported to our small JSON format with the Python tool), so the same model can be run on another site or with better numbers.

What is creative

We turned the route map around: instead of the shortest path, the app draws where the crew can still get home, as walk-back contours over real terrain. Showing every result as a range, a one-click sensitivity test of every assumption, and a first-person helmet view with a HUD computed from the elevation model are our own additions.

Honest by design

Walking speed in a suit is the weakest number, so every result is also shown for 1.7-3.6 km/h, and a one-click sensitivity test re-runs the whole model with each assumption changed (the reserve and the walking speed matter most; roughness and shielding barely matter). We checked the terrain model against what Perseverance itself measured along its real drive: the correlation of slope with the rover's measured tilt is 0.83 on the 40 m grid the app opens with and 0.87 on the 20 m grid. On the default plan the farthest stop is 58 minutes from home against a 120-minute limit, and one stop, 215 minutes away, is refused. The four demo stops were picked by us from the terrain; they are not NASA science targets. The limits are written down in the app and in the README: no individual rocks, an uneven mosaic, assumed walking speeds, and a radiation baseline measured at Gale crater.

How it is used

One HTML file (about 9 MB), no server and no network access: it runs on a laptop, a tablet or a phone, so it can serve as a habitat or tablet display, and the helmet view shows the HUD idea. The screen is a full-screen map with zoom and pan, a side panel (briefing, plan, places search, layers with a thumbnail for each layer) and a first-visit tour. Its layout follows the interaction pattern of NASA's Mars Trek web viewer; none of Trek's code, data, images or branding is used. Python and JavaScript versions of the model give the same numbers (checked by automated tests).

Tools

Python (NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image), plain JavaScript and Canvas; tests in Node.js and headless Chromium. Built with an AI assistant (Claude Code); see the next section.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

  • Code and text: the source code (Python and JavaScript), the automated tests, the documentation and this description were written by an AI assistant (Anthropic's Claude, used through Claude Code) working from a team member's instructions. A team member chose the challenge, directed the work, and downloaded and supplied the real datasets.
  • Images and video: none is SI-generated, so no SI watermark applies. All pictures are screenshots of the app or renderings of NASA and USGS data; the helmet view is computed from the elevation model; the demo video is screen captures of the app, arranged and captioned by a script (no people, no voice).
  • Audio: the video soundtrack was composed by the AI assistant as code: a script that computes the music and sound effects from sine waves, noise and echoes, with no recordings, samples or audio-generation model.
  • Data: all datasets are real NASA and USGS data. No data was invented by SI; the 40 m and 20 m grids were computed from the real rasters by a script that the AI assistant wrote (tools/hirise_window.py in the repository).
  • NASA branding: the app and the video contain no NASA logo, flag or mission patch, and nothing of NASA's branding is modified.
  • Review: the code has not been reviewed line by line by a human domain expert. Confidence rests on the automated tests (163 Python, 23 JavaScript core, 10 compatibility and 33 browser tests), on the Python and JavaScript versions giving the same numbers, and on a comparison with the rover's own measurements.
  • Timeline: the model, the tests and the real-data processing were prepared between 5 and 8 November 2026, before the event. During the event, on 15 November, the map viewer was redesigned after NASA's Mars Trek and the demo video, screenshots, slides and this text were re-made. Full detail: AI_DISCLOSURE.md and CHANGELOG.md in the repository.
